cse-2022-cs-13.approach: Check each claim against the hierarchy regular ⊂ DCFL ⊂ CFL ⊂ recursive ⊂ RE and the standard closure facts.

steps.title: Subsets of RE languages
steps.body: $\Sigma^*$ is RE (even regular), and **every** language over $\Sigma$ — including undecidable ones such as the complement of the halting language — is a subset of it. So (A) is false.

steps.title: L and its complement both RE
steps.body: Run the recognisers for $L$ and $\overline{L}$ in parallel on input $w$. Exactly one of them accepts, so the combined machine always halts: $L$ is recursive. (B) is true.

steps.title: Complement of a CFL
steps.body: Every CFL is recursive (CYK decides membership). Recursive languages are closed under complement, so $\overline{L}$ is recursive even though it need not be context-free. (C) is true.

steps.title: Intersection of regular languages
steps.body: Regular languages are closed under intersection, so $L_1 \cap L_2$ is regular, and every regular language is a DCFL. (D) is true.

optionAnalysis.reason: False: $\Sigma^*$ is RE but has non-recursive (even non-RE) subsets.
True: running both recognisers in parallel gives a decider (Post's theorem).
True: CFLs are recursive and recursive languages are closed under complement.
True: $L_1 \cap L_2$ is regular, hence deterministic context-free.

pitfalls: Confusing "complement of a CFL is a CFL" (false) with "complement of a CFL is recursive" (true).
cse-2022-cs-13.verification: Matches the official key B, C, D.

cse-2022-cs-14.approach: Recall what write-back and write-through actually do on hits, misses and evictions; the question asks for the FALSE statements.

steps.title: Dirty bit
steps.body: A write-through cache updates memory on every write, so its blocks are never "dirty" — it needs no dirty bit. Only WB needs one, so (A) is **false**.

steps.title: Write hits in WB
steps.body: Write-back only updates the cache on a hit and marks the block dirty; memory is written only when the block is evicted. (B) is **false**.

steps.title: Evictions in WT
steps.body: In WT memory already holds the latest data, so an evicted block is simply dropped — no transfer. (C) is **true**.

steps.title: Read misses in WB
steps.body: A read miss brings in a new block; if the LRU victim in that set is dirty, it must be written back first. So a read miss *can* evict a dirty block and (D) is **false**.

optionAnalysis.reason: FALSE (selected): write-through blocks never become dirty, so WT has no dirty bit.
FALSE (selected): WB writes to memory only on eviction of a dirty block, not on every write hit.
TRUE (not selected): WT memory is always up to date, so evictions transfer nothing.
FALSE (selected): the replaced block on a read miss may be dirty and then must be written back.

pitfalls: The question asks for FALSE statements — the selected options are the false ones.
cse-2022-cs-14.verification: Matches the official key A, B, D.

cse-2022-cs-15.approach: Division $R/S$ returns the $x$ values paired with every tuple of $S$; the divisor must be the set of all brands. Option B is the textbook expansion of division into ×, − and Π.

steps.title: Direct division (A)
steps.body: $\Pi_{eId,bId}(Own) / \Pi_{bId}(Brand)$ gives every $eId$ that appears with **every** $bId$ of $Brand$ — exactly "owns all brands". The outer $\Pi_{eId}$ changes nothing. (A) is correct.

steps.title: Division via difference (B)
steps.body: $\Pi_{eId}(Own) \times \Pi_{bId}(Brand)$ = every (owner, brand) pair that *should* exist. Subtracting $\Pi_{eId,bId}(Own)$ leaves the **missing** pairs; projecting $eId$ gives owners missing at least one brand. Removing them from $\Pi_{eId}(Own)$ leaves owners of all brands. (B) is correct.

steps.title: Wrong divisor (C)
steps.body: $\Pi_{bId}(Own)$ is only the brands someone owns. If a brand exists in $Brand$ that nobody owns, (C) still returns employees owning all *owned* brands — wrong in general.

steps.title: Product before division (D)
steps.body: $\Pi_{eId}(Own) \times \Pi_{bId}(Own)$ pairs every owner with every owned brand, so after dividing by $Brand$ it returns either all owners (when every brand is owned) or nobody — not the required set.

optionAnalysis.reason: Correct: standard division by the set of all brands.
Correct: the expansion R/S = Π(R) − Π((Π(R) × S) − R).
Wrong: divides by owned brands only; fails if some brand is owned by nobody.
Wrong: the cross product destroys who-owns-what, so the result is all owners or nobody.

pitfalls: Using $\Pi_{bId}(Own)$ instead of $\Pi_{bId}(Brand)$ as the divisor.
cse-2022-cs-15.verification: Tested with Brand = {1,2,3}, Own = {(e1,1),(e1,2),(e1,3),(e2,1)}: A and B return {e1}; with brand 3 unowned C returns e1 too but should be empty; D returns {e1, e2} when all brands are owned.

cse-2022-cs-16.approach: Test each statement against the four Coffman conditions and the difference between single-instance and multi-instance resources.

steps.title: Circular wait
steps.body: Mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption and circular wait are all **necessary** for deadlock. (A) is true.

steps.title: Cycle with multi-instance resources
steps.body: With several instances per resource a cycle is necessary but not sufficient — another instance may be released and break the wait. (B) is false.

steps.title: Unsafe state
steps.body: Unsafe only means deadlock is *possible*; processes may release resources or request less than their maximum. (C) is false.

steps.title: Only assignment edges
steps.body: No request edges means no process is waiting for anything, so no process can be deadlocked. (D) is true.

optionAnalysis.reason: True: circular wait is one of the four necessary conditions.
False: with multiple instances a cycle does not guarantee deadlock.
False: unsafe ≠ deadlocked; deadlock may still be avoided.
True: no request edges ⇒ no waiting ⇒ no deadlock.

cse-2022-cs-17.approach: Use cancellation laws for (A), $x = x^{-1}$ for (B), the cyclic group of prime order for (C), and the fact that subgroups inherit commutativity for (D).

steps.title: (A) and (B)
steps.body:
(A): $xyxy = xxyy$; cancel $x$ on the left and $y$ on the right: $yx = xy$. True.

(B): $x^2 = 1 \Rightarrow x = x^{-1}$ for every $x$. Then $xy = (xy)^{-1} = y^{-1}x^{-1} = yx$. True.

steps.title: (C) and (D)
steps.body:
(C): a group of order 2 is $\{1, a\}$ with $a^2 = 1$; any two elements commute. True.

(D): a subgroup uses the same operation on a subset, so $xy = yx$ still holds — a subgroup of a commutative group **must** be commutative. False.

optionAnalysis.reason: True: cancellation gives yx = xy.
True: every element is its own inverse, so xy = (xy)^{-1} = yx.
True: order 2 (prime) ⇒ cyclic ⇒ abelian.
False: commutativity is inherited by every subgroup.

cse-2022-cs-17.verification: Matches the official key A, B, C.

cse-2022-cs-18.approach: In heap-array layout node $i$ has children $2i+1$ and $2i+2$. Find the largest element by walking right from the root, then step back with in-order predecessors.

steps.title: Shape of the tree
steps.body: Levels 0–8 are full: $2^9 - 1 = 511$ nodes (indices 0–510). The last level holds $1000 - 511 = 489$ nodes: indices 511–999.

steps.title: Largest element
steps.body: Walk right: $0 \to 2 \to 6 \to 14 \to 30 \to 62 \to 126 \to 254 \to 510$. Next would be $2\cdot510+2 = 1022 > 999$, and the left child $1021 > 999$ too. So index **510** is the maximum (a leaf).

steps.title: 2nd and 3rd largest
steps.body:
510 has no left subtree and is the right child of 254 (since $2\cdot254+2 = 510$), so its predecessor is **254**.

The predecessor of 254 is the maximum of its left subtree: left child $2\cdot254+1 = 509$; its right child $2\cdot509+2 = 1020 > 999$ does not exist, so 509 is that maximum.

3rd largest is at index **509**.

pitfalls: Assuming the rightmost path reaches the last level — the last level is only partly filled, so it stops at level 8.
cse-2022-cs-18.verification: In-order around index 254: subtree(509) < 254 < 510, and 509 is a leaf (1019, 1020 > 999), so the order of the top three is 510, 254, 509.

cse-2022-cs-19.approach: closure(I₀) adds nothing (the dots are before + or at the end), so goto on + just advances the dot in $S \to S\bullet+R$ and closes over $R$.

steps.title: closure(I₀)
steps.body: In $[S' \to S\bullet]$ the dot is at the end; in $[S \to S\bullet + R]$ it is before the terminal $+$. Neither adds items, so $closure(I_0) = I_0$.

steps.title: goto on +
steps.body: Only $[S \to S\bullet + R]$ has $+$ after the dot. Kernel: $[S \to S + \bullet R]$.

steps.title: Close the kernel
steps.body:
Dot before $R$: add $R \to \bullet R * P$ and $R \to \bullet P$. Dot before $P$: add $P \to \bullet (S)$ and $P \to \bullet id$.

$$\{S \to S+\bullet R,\ R \to \bullet R*P,\ R \to \bullet P,\ P \to \bullet(S),\ P \to \bullet id\}$$

That is $1 + 2 + 2 = 5$ items.

pitfalls: Forgetting to close over $P$ after adding $R \to \bullet P$.
cse-2022-cs-19.verification: This is the familiar "S → S+•R" state of the expression grammar, which has 5 items.

steps.title: Best split

cse-2022-cs-21.approach: Find the attributes that never appear on a right-hand side — every key must contain them. Here that is AB, and AB alone is a key, so superkeys are AB plus any subset of the other 3 attributes.

steps.title: Closure of AB
steps.body: $AB^+$: $AB \to C$ gives $ABC$; $BC \to D$ gives $ABCD$; $C \to E$ gives $ABCDE$. So $AB$ is a superkey.

steps.title: AB is the only candidate key
steps.body: $A$ and $B$ appear on no right-hand side, so every superkey must contain both. Hence $AB$ is the unique candidate key.

steps.title: Count superkeys
steps.body: Superkeys $= AB \cup X$ for any $X \subseteq \{C, D, E\}$: $2^3 = 8$.

cse-2022-cs-26.approach: Split $a_n = 1 + [n \text{ odd}]\,n$. The "1" part gives $\frac{1}{1-x}$; the odd part is $x\frac{d}{dx}$ of $\frac{x}{1-x^2}$.

steps.title: Split the sequence
steps.body: For odd $n$: $a_n = n + 1 = 1 + n$; for even $n$: $a_n = 1$. So $A(x) = \sum_{n\ge0} x^n + \sum_{n \text{ odd}} n x^n = \dfrac{1}{1-x} + \sum_{n\text{ odd}} n x^n$.

steps.title: Odd part
steps.body:
$\sum_{n\text{ odd}} x^n = \dfrac{x}{1-x^2}$. Then

$$\sum_{n\text{ odd}} n x^n = x\frac{d}{dx}\left(\frac{x}{1-x^2}\right) = x\cdot\frac{(1-x^2) + 2x^2}{(1-x^2)^2} = \frac{x(1+x^2)}{(1-x^2)^2}.$$

Wrong: $2x/(1-x^2)^2 = 2x + 4x^3 + \dots$ gives $a_1 = 3$.
Wrong: $x/(1-x^2)^2 = x + 2x^3 + \dots$ gives $a_3 = 3$, but $a_3 = 4$.
